newsitem.title: UK: British movie makers see big boost from tax break.
newsitem.headline: British movie makers see big boost from tax break.

text.p: British movie makers on Thursday hailed new tax breaks for films as a major step toward transforming Britain's cottage film industry into a consistent force in world cinema.
The Labour government on Wednesday said it would allow companies to write off the entire cost of films worth up to 15 million pounds ($25.1 million) right after the movies are made.
The plan should cut the cost of making movies in Britain by about 10 percent and boost investment in the local film industry beyond its current record levels, industry experts said.
Besides attracting foreign investment, the tax breaks should also lure in local investors who have tended to shy away from the risky movie business.

"In the last decade, there's been very little confidence from City (local) investors a propos the film industry," said Eric Fellner, co-head of PolyGram's Working Title Films, which produced hits like "Four Weddings and a Funeral."
"This might start to reinstate that confidence. Confidence is what brings the big money into the film business," he added.
The new tax break scheme came less than two months after a handful of film companies won 90 million pounds of national lottery funds to boost their output over the next six years.

"Britain is regarded as a good place to make films already now, and if you add (the tax break), I think it may make all the difference," said Premila Hoon, head of media and entertainment finance at investment bank Guinness Mahon.

According to estimates by the British Screen Advisory Council (BSAC), the tax breaks should create 11,000 new jobs in the first year and boost investment in the industry by 30 percent, or about 140 million pounds, over 1995 levels.
Unlike Britain's previous 100 percent tax break scheme, the new plan lets movie makers write off a film's costs in the first year after its completion rather than stretching it out over three years.
This difference was expected to make it easier for companies to take advantage of the write-offs and allow them to spend more on their movies.
"That will be great. That means the production values will rise, and we should be able to compete more," said BSAC director Fiona Clarke-Hackston.
"This makes it far more of a level playing field when compared with other countries," she added. ($ = 0.596 British Pounds)
